What konfig.ts is, what it gives you, what it is not, and what you need to run it.

import { Aside, Diagnostics } from "@/components/docs"

konfig.ts renders Kubernetes manifests and Argo CD `Application` resources from TypeScript. It is a set of `@konfig.ts/*` packages built on [Effect](https://effect.website/), plus a `konfig` CLI that loads your `.ts` sources, renders them, and writes YAML into a directory Argo CD can sync.

The point is not YAML generation by itself. konfig.ts wires two layers of an application from one TypeScript source:

- The **manifest layer**: Deployments, Services, Secrets, Helm releases, Argo CD Applications, and the dependency graph between them.
- The **runtime config layer**: the environment variables your process reads at startup, decoded with Effect `Config`.

Because both layers come from the same declarations, the mistakes you would otherwise discover at `argocd sync` time (a workload referencing a Secret nobody created, an env var read in code but missing from the pod spec, a chart pinned by version but not by digest) become TypeScript errors or fail-closed render errors.

## What you get

- **A dependency graph checked at the type level.** Modules declare what they need (`Dep.Need<...>`) and what they provide (`Dep.Provide<...>`). `AppOfApps.fromModules` composes them, and `AppOfApps.entrypoint` refuses to compile until every need has a provider. See [Dependency graph](/konfig.ts/docs/concepts/dependency-graph/).
- **One env contract for both sides.** `Secret.define`, `Literal.define`, and `Downward.define` from `@konfig.ts/env` produce atoms that `Environment.bind` turns into a Deployment env block and Secret resources, and that `Environment.runtime` decodes inside the running process. Rename a variable once and both sides move.
- **Deterministic YAML and structural diffs.** Output uses stable key ordering (YAML 1.1, deterministic field sort, Argo CD friendly). `konfig diff` compares rendered output against a baseline structurally, so reordered keys and multi-document files do not show up as noise.
- **Secret backends as typed values.** sops, sealed-secrets, and external-secrets each lower a `Secret.define` to the matching custom resource, with schema validation on the binary's output. Whether a backend requires a source file is encoded in its type, so forgetting the source for a sops backend is a compile error.
- **Helm with digest verification.** `Helm.release({ digest })` hashes the cached chart tarball on every pull and every cache hit. A chart whose bytes change fails the next render.

## What konfig.ts is not

- **Not a kustomize replacement.** If you have hand-written YAML and want to overlay it, konfig.ts is the wrong tool. It owns the manifest source.
- **Not a runtime mutator.** It emits manifests; Argo CD or `kubectl` applies them. There is no admission controller and no operator.
- **Not a higher-level platform abstraction.** No Crossplane, no OAM, no "Service" model that hides Deployment, Service, and Ingress. `Workload.web` is a helper that emits those resources explicitly.
- **Not a Helm replacement.** It shells out to `helm template`. Charts you depend on stay charts; each templated document is lifted into the render as a `RawYaml` manifest.

## Requirements

<Aside type="caution" title="Exact Effect pin">
Every `@konfig.ts/*` package is built against Effect 4 (release candidate) and declares an exact peer version, currently `effect@4.0.0-rc.109`. The pin is exact on purpose: the release-candidate line makes breaking changes between builds, and a caret range would surface as `ERESOLVE` conflicts instead of a working install. Install exactly the version the packages declare. The pin relaxes once Effect ships a stable 4.x.
</Aside>

The `konfig` CLI imports your `.ts` sources at runtime, so it needs a TypeScript-capable runtime:

| Runtime | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Bun | Recommended, runs `.ts` with no flags |
| Node >= 23.6 | Works, native type stripping |
| Node 22.6 to 23.5 | Works with `--experimental-strip-types` |
| `tsx` | Works: `tsx node_modules/.bin/konfig ...` |

Rendering Helm-based modules calls the `helm` binary; `konfig validate --strict` calls `kubeconform`. Type-checking and in-memory renders of manifest-only projects need neither.

`@konfig.ts/argocd` turns each module into one Argo CD `Application` and writes a root directory of `Application` CRs that a single Argo CD root app can sync. This guide walks from `Application.define` to the directory layout Argo CD needs.

## The pieces

- `Application.define({ name, namespace, source, build, provides?, project?, syncPolicy?, annotations? })` builds one Application. `name` and `namespace` must be string literals (`Application.LiteralName<T>`), which is what lets the dependency graph reason about them at the type level.
- `Application.target` is the target you hand to `Module.fixedNs` / `Module.dynamicNs`. It adds `source` as a per-call argument and `project`, `syncPolicy`, `annotations` as module config.
- `Application.make(opts)` is the plain value constructor (no dependency graph); `AppOfApps.fromModules` calls it for you.
- `AppOfApps.fromModules({ target, defaults, modules, name? })` composes the module layers, resolves every `Dep.Need`, and yields an `AppOfAppsResult` (`{ name, target, defaults, apps }`). `name` defaults to `"apps"`.
- `AppOfApps.entrypoint(program)` is the compile-time gate: it accepts the program only when no residual need is left. See [Dependency graph](/konfig.ts/docs/concepts/dependency-graph/).

## Two shapes: target and source

`target` describes where the whole environment lives in git and is used to build the child `Application` CRs:

```ts
interface AppOfAppsTarget {
  readonly repoURL: string
  readonly branch: string
  readonly rootPath: string            // directory Argo's root app syncs
  readonly controllerNamespace?: string // metadata.namespace of the CRs, default "argocd"
}
```

`source` is per module and becomes `spec.source` of that module's `Application`:

```ts
interface ArgoSource {
  readonly repoURL: string
  readonly targetRevision: string
  readonly path: string
}
```

The example builds `source` from `target` with a small helper so every child points at `<rootPath>/<module name>`. Here is the whole entrypoint of the production environment.

`cluster.repositoryUrl` comes from a plain TypeScript constant shared by every environment.

## Sync order with `Sync.*`

`Sync` produces `argocd.argoproj.io/*` annotation records you spread into `annotations` (of `Application.define`, `Module.fixedNs`, or a resource's `metadata.annotations`):

- `Sync.wave(n)` sets `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave`.
- `Sync.hook(phase)` sets `argocd.argoproj.io/hook` with `phase` in `PreSync | Sync | PostSync | SyncFail | PostDelete`.
- `Sync.options(["Prune=false", ...])` sets `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options` (comma-joined).

The example places the sops operator at wave -2, secrets and infrastructure at -1, and workloads at the default 0.

<Snippet file="infra/modules/sops-operator.ts" startAt="export const defineSopsOperator" title="infra/modules/sops-operator.ts" />

## Defaults and per-app overrides

`defaults` applies to every child CR: `destination.server` (falls back to `https://kubernetes.default.svc`), `project` (falls back to `"default"`), and `syncPolicy`. A module's own `project` or `syncPolicy` wins; `syncPolicy.automated` and `retry` are merged field by field, `syncOptions` is replaced whole.

## What gets written

`konfig build <env>` renders each Application's manifests into `<outDir.manifests>/<env>/<app name>/` and writes one `Application` CR per module into `<outDir.manifests>/<env>/<result name>/` (`apps/` unless you pass `name`). The CR filename is `applicationCRFilename(app)`, which is `Application-<name>.yaml` with `.` and `/` replaced by `-`. The CR itself comes from `serializeApplicationCR({ app, target, defaults })`; `emitApplicationCR` wraps the same YAML in a `Manifest` when you want to compose it further.

For the example above the tree looks like this:

```text
.generated/manifests/prod/
  apps/
    Application-api.yaml
    Application-postgres.yaml
    ...
  api/
    Deployment-api.yaml
    Service-api.yaml
    ...
  postgres/
    ...
```

<Aside type="note" title="rootPath is a git path, outDir is a filesystem path">
`target.rootPath` is what ends up in `spec.source.path` of the CRs and must be the path of the rendered directory inside the repository Argo CD clones (`./infra/k8s/manifests/prod` in the example). `outDir.manifests` in `konfig.json` is where the CLI writes locally. Keep the two pointing at the same committed directory.
</Aside>

## Pointing Argo CD at it

<Steps>

1. Render and commit the output.

   ```bash
   konfig build prod
   git add infra/k8s/manifests/prod && git commit -m "render prod"
   ```

2. Create one root `Application` by hand (or with `Application.make`) whose `spec.source.path` is `<rootPath>/<result name>`, for example `infra/k8s/manifests/prod/apps`, on `target.branch`.

3. Sync the root app. Argo CD creates the child Applications from the CRs in that directory; each child syncs its own `source.path` in sync-wave order.

</Steps>

Because every child CR is generated from the same `target`, changing `branch` or `rootPath` in one place moves the whole environment. Removing a module from `modules` removes its CR on the next build, and with `automated.prune` in `defaults.syncPolicy` Argo CD deletes the child.

import { Aside, Steps, Snippet } from "@/components/docs"

`@konfig.ts/docker` emits Dockerfiles for apps in a Bun/npm/pnpm/yarn workspace monorepo. You write one `docker.ts` next to the app; the package resolves the app's transitive workspace closure and writes the `COPY` lists for you. It emits files only: no building, pushing, or tagging.

## The spec

`Docker.app(spec)` wraps a `DockerSpec`, an Effect Schema struct decoded on load. The example's API service:

<Snippet file="apps/api/docker.ts" startAt="export default Docker.app" title="apps/api/docker.ts" lang="ts" />

Fields:

- `target`: workspace directory relative to the monorepo root.
- `runner`: the production stage. `workdir`, `copy`, and `cmd` are required. `production: true` adds a `prod-deps` stage that trims the root `package.json` workspaces to the closure and runs `bun install --production` (or the package manager's equivalent). Optional: `env`, `expose` (number or array), `entrypoint`, `user`, `healthcheck`, `platform`, `baseImage`, `removePaths`.
- `dev`: single-stage dev image. `cmd` required; `env`, `expose`, `workdir` optional.
- `packageManager`, `runtime`, `build`, `sharedRootFiles`: optional overrides, described below.

Env values are validated against a secret heuristic (`sk_` prefixes, PEM headers, long base64 strings). A value that looks like a secret fails decoding: runtime secrets belong to `Environment.bind`, not to an image layer.

## Atoms

Each option is a tagged value built with a constructor under `Docker.*`:

| Family | Constructors |
| --- | --- |
| `Docker.copy` | `builderArtifact({ src, dst, chown? })`, `workspaceSource(name)`, `workspaceSourceAll()`, `path({ src, dst, from?, chown? })` |
| `Docker.runtime` | `bun({ alpine? })`, `node({ alpine? })` |
| `Docker.pm` | `bun()`, `npm()`, `pnpm()`, `yarn({ variant? })` |
| `Docker.build` | `script(name)`, `command(argv)`, `none()` |
| `Docker.healthcheck` | `httpGet({ path, port, interval?, timeout?, retries?, startPeriod? })`, `command({ argv, ... })` |
| `Docker.user` | `nonRoot({ uid?, gid?, name? })`, `root()` |
| `Docker.platform` | `linuxAmd64()`, `linuxArm64()`, `multi(values)` |

`Docker.copy.workspaceSourceAll()` copies the source of every workspace in the closure into the runner (needed for Bun's `workspace:*` links and export conditions); `workspaceSource("@example/env-contracts")` copies one; `builderArtifact` copies a build output such as `dist` from the `builder` stage. When `runner.baseImage` is set, nothing is copied automatically and `runner.copy` must list everything.

`packageManager` defaults to detection from the root `package.json` and lockfile; `runtime` defaults to match; `build` defaults to `Docker.build.script("build")` when the target has that script and to `none()` otherwise (`BuildScriptMissing` if you name a script that does not exist).

## Runtime version from engines

The runner image tag is read from the app's `package.json` `engines.<runtime>` field (`engines.bun` or `engines.node`). The example declares `"engines": { "bun": "1.3.5" }`, so the runner is `oven/bun:1.3.5-alpine`. A missing field is a hard `EngineVersionMissing` error rather than a floating `latest`.

## Workspace closure resolution

`findRoot(targetAbs)` walks up to the nearest `package.json` with a `workspaces` field (`MonorepoRootNotFound` otherwise). `closureOf` follows `dependencies` and `peerDependencies` that use a workspace protocol (`workspace:*`, `link:`, ...) and rejects cycles (`CircularWorkspaceDep`). `devDependencies` are deliberately excluded so build-only tooling never lands in the runner. The closure drives every generated `COPY`: the `deps` stage copies every workspace's `package.json` so the lockfile resolves, while `builder`, `prod-deps`, and `runner` copy only closure members. The root `package.json`, lockfile, and package-manager config are copied automatically; extra root files an install needs (an `.npmrc`, a patches directory) go in `sharedRootFiles`, and naming one that does not exist is `SharedRootFileMissing`.

## Stages of the production Dockerfile

`base → deps → builder → runner`, plus `prod-deps` between `builder` and `runner` when `runner.production` is `true`:

- `base`: `FROM <runtime>:<engines version>[-alpine]`.
- `deps`: copies every workspace `package.json` plus the lockfile and installs with scripts disabled.
- `builder`: copies `node_modules` from `deps`, copies closure sources, runs the build atom.
- `prod-deps` (optional): rewrites `workspaces` to the closure, drops `devDependencies`, installs with `--production`.
- `runner`: non-root user, `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `COPY --chown` of the declared artifacts, `HEALTHCHECK`, `USER`, `CMD`.

Dev is `base → dev`: one install with scripts enabled, closure sources copied in, `NODE_ENV=development`, the watch-mode `cmd`, no user or healthcheck.

Every generated file starts with a header carrying the marker `# konfig-managed: @konfig.ts/docker`, the spec path, and a hash of the spec. `konfig docker write` refuses to overwrite a file without that marker unless you pass `--force`.

<Steps>

1. Preview to stdout.

   ```bash
   konfig docker preview apps/api            # both files
   konfig docker preview apps/api --prod-only
   ```

2. Write `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.dev` next to the target (`--out-dir` to place them elsewhere, `--force` to replace unmanaged files).

`@konfig.ts/core` defines the file shape as an Effect Schema and decodes it strictly (unknown keys fail):

```ts
// packages/core/src/images.ts
export const EnvImages = Schema.Record(Schema.String, Schema.String)
export const ImagesConfig = Schema.Struct({
  envs: Schema.Record(Schema.String, EnvImages)
})
```

The file lives at `<konfig.json dir>/<root>/images.json`. Values are opaque strings: the schema does not parse them, so a project picks a convention. The `konfig set` help text suggests full refs (`ghcr.io/<org>/<app>:<sha>`); the example's build modules take `registry` and `tag` separately, so the example convention is tag-only with the registry coming from `cluster.ts`.

```json title="images.json"

	"envs": {
		"prod": { "api": "1.0.0", "worker": "1.0.0" },
		"staging": { "api": "sha-3f2a9c1", "worker": "sha-3f2a9c1" }
	}
}
```

Helpers, all exported from `@konfig.ts/core`:

| Helper | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `decodeImagesSync(u)` / `decodeImagesEffect(u)` | Strict decode of the parsed JSON |
| `imagesFor({ cfg, env })` | Env record, throws `ImagesEnvMissing` |
| `lookupEnvEffect({ cfg, env })` | Same, as an Effect failing with `ImagesEnvMissing` |
| `requireImage({ e, app, envName })` | One value, throws `ImagesAppMissing` |
| `requireImageEffect(...)` | Same, as an Effect failing with `ImagesAppMissing` |
| `lookupEnv({ cfg, env })` | Env record or `undefined` |

`ImagesEnvMissing` carries `{ env }`, `ImagesAppMissing` carries `{ env, app }`. Both are `Data.TaggedError`s, so an env entry that reads the file fails with a named error rather than rendering a workload with `image: undefined`.

## How images reach a workload

A build module is a dependency-graph anchor: it emits no manifests and provides `Dep.Image` for one app via `Dep.provideImage({ app, registry, tag })`, which brands `${registry}/${app}:${tag}` as `BuiltImageRef<"api">`.

<Snippet file="infra/modules/builds.ts" startAt="export const defineApiBuild" endBefore="export const defineWorkerBuild" title="infra/modules/builds.ts" />

The consuming module does `yield* Dep.Image("api")` inside its build and passes the branded string to `Container.define`.

<Snippet file="infra/modules/api.ts" startAt="export const defineApi" endBefore="      const bound" title="infra/modules/api.ts" />

If no module in `AppOfApps.fromModules({ modules })` provides `Image "api"`, `AppOfApps.entrypoint` fails to compile with `_konfig_unsatisfied`; see [Worked failures](/konfig.ts/docs/guides/worked-failures/).

## Reading images.json in the env entry

The example passes literal tags to `defineApiBuild` for offline reproducibility. To drive them from `images.json`, read the file in the env entry and hand the value to the build module. The env entry runs at build time, so a synchronous read is fine here.

```ts title="infra/envs/prod.ts"
import { decodeImagesSync, imagesFor, requireImage } from "@konfig.ts/core"
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs"

const images = imagesFor({
  cfg: decodeImagesSync(JSON.parse(readFileSync("images.json", "utf8"))),
  env: "prod"
})

const apiBuild = defineApiBuild({
  name: "api-build",
  source: src("api-build"),
  registry: "ghcr.io/example",
  tag: requireImage({ e: images, app: "api", envName: "prod" })
})
```

A missing `prod` block throws `ImagesEnvMissing`; a missing `api` key throws `ImagesAppMissing`. Both surface as an `EnvLoadError` from `konfig build` with the tagged cause, and no manifest is written.

## Promoting from CI

`konfig set <env> <app> <image>` performs a schema-validated read, replaces one key, and writes the file back tab-indented. It refuses an env that is not already present (`SetUnknownEnv`) and never creates the file (`ImagesFileError`), so a typo in the env name cannot silently add a new environment.

<Steps>

1. Build and push the image in your CI job; capture the tag (a git SHA works well).

2. Update the manifest source and re-render.

   ```bash
   konfig set staging api sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}
   konfig build staging
   ```

3. Commit both `images.json` and the rendered manifests, then push. Argo CD picks up the change on its next refresh.

   ```bash
   git add images.json .generated/manifests/staging
   git commit -m "promote api to sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7} (staging)"
   git push
   ```

4. Promote to production by repeating with `prod`, ideally from a job that requires approval.

</Steps>

<Aside type="tip" title="One diff to review">
Because `Dep.Image` is the only path from `images.json` to a pod spec, the rendered diff of a promotion is exactly the `image:` lines of the affected workloads. `konfig diff staging` shows it structurally before you commit.
</Aside>

End to end with @konfig.ts/sops. Define the Secret contract, commit an encrypted SopsSecret, choose passthrough or re-encrypt, install the operator, bind in a module, and rotate.

import { Aside, Steps, Snippet } from "@/components/docs"

`@konfig.ts/sops` lowers a `Secret.define` contract to a `SopsSecret` custom resource that the in-cluster [sops-secrets-operator](https://github.com/isindir/sops-secrets-operator) decrypts into a native `Secret`. Ciphertext is the only thing that ever reaches the rendered manifests. This guide follows the example project's `db-creds` secret from contract to rotation.

## Steps

<Steps>

1. **Define the contract.** `Secret.define` names the Kubernetes Secret, its namespace, and a map from key to env var name. The same value is imported by the workload module (to bind) and by the app (to decode at runtime), so a rename moves both sides.

   <Snippet file="shared/env-contracts/src/secrets.ts" startAt="export const dbCreds" endBefore="export const s3Creds" title="shared/env-contracts/src/secrets.ts" />

2. **Create the encrypted file.** The committed file is a complete `SopsSecret` CR encrypted with `sops`; only `stringData` (and `data`) values are ciphertext, `metadata` and the `sops:` block stay readable. Write the plaintext CR, then run `sops --encrypt --age <recipient> --encrypted-regex '^(data|stringData)$' --in-place infra/secrets/SopsSecret-db-creds.yaml`. The result looks like this (the example ships fake ciphertext so it renders offline):

   <Snippet file="infra/secrets/SopsSecret-db-creds.yaml" lang="yaml" title="infra/secrets/SopsSecret-db-creds.yaml" />

   `spec.secretTemplates[].name` must equal `metadata.name`, and both should equal the `name` in `Secret.define`; the keys under `stringData` must cover every key of the contract's `env` map.

3. **Install the operator** as its own Application at an early sync wave, so the CRD and controller exist before any `SopsSecret` is applied. The operator reads its age key from a Secret you create out of band (`sops-age` in the example).

   <Snippet file="infra/modules/sops-operator.ts" startAt="export const defineSopsOperator" title="infra/modules/sops-operator.ts" />

4. **Bind in the module.** `Environment.bind` takes the env contract and one backend per secret member. `Sops.passthrough({ file })` reads the encrypted file at render time and emits it as the manifest; `bound.manifests` carries the CRs and `bound.envVars` the `secretKeyRef` entries for the container.

   <Snippet file="infra/modules/api.ts" startAt="      const bound = Environment.bind" endBefore="      const apiContainer" title="infra/modules/api.ts" />

   For a single secret outside an env contract, `Secret.bind({ secret, backend })` does the same and returns `{ ref, envVars, manifest, refLayer }`; `image-pulls.ts` uses it for the registry credential.

5. **Render.** `konfig build prod` writes `SopsSecret-db-creds.yaml` into the `api` Application's directory. Argo CD applies it, the operator decrypts it in-cluster, and the pod's `DATABASE_URL` env var resolves from the resulting native `Secret`.

</Steps>

## passthrough versus backend + source

`Sops` exposes three functions:

| | `Sops.passthrough({ file })` | `Sops.backend({ recipients, type? })` + `Sops.source({ file, keys, extract? })` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs `sops` binary at build | No | Yes (`sops --decrypt` then `sops --encrypt`) |
| Needs the private key at build | No | Yes, to decrypt the source |
| `source` in the bind | Optional (`requiresSource: false`) | Required by the type (`requiresSource: true`) |
| Output | The committed file, verified and restamped | A fresh `SopsSecret` re-encrypted to `recipients` |

Use `passthrough` when the file is already encrypted for the cluster and CI should not hold a decryption key. Use `backend` + `source` when the source of truth is encrypted for developers and CI re-encrypts to the cluster's recipient, or when the source is a different backend altogether (`Sops.source` yields `Redacted` values any `SecretBackend` can consume, for example sealed-secrets).

`recipients` accepts `age`, `kms`, `gcpKms`, `azureKv`, and `pgp` arrays. `type` sets `secretTemplates[].type` and defaults to `Opaque`.

Restamping: `passthrough` rewrites `metadata.namespace` and `name` to the bound values only when the file's `sops.mac_only_encrypted` is `true`. Otherwise the MAC covers those fields and konfig refuses to change them, so name the file's metadata to match the contract.

## Fail closed

Every emitted CR passes through the same pipeline: parse YAML, decode against the `SopsSecret` schema, then check that each value under `stringData` and `data` starts with `ENC[` (honouring `sops.encrypted_regex` when present). A value without the marker fails the render with a `RenderError` whose cause is `SopsUnencryptedValueError`, and nothing is written for that Application:

```text
Sops.passthrough(app/db-creds): refusing to emit, value for "password" is not sops-encrypted (missing ENC[ marker)
```

The same check runs on `sops --encrypt` output in `backend` mode, so a misconfigured `encrypted_regex` cannot produce a plaintext CR.

## Rotation

Rotating a value means re-encrypting the file (`sops --rotate` or edit and re-encrypt), committing, and rendering. The manifest changes, Argo CD applies it, and the operator updates the native `Secret`. Whether pods pick the change up depends on how you asked for it:

- `Workload.web({ reloader: "stakater" })` adds `reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true"` to the Deployment, so a running [Reloader](https://github.com/stakater/Reloader) restarts pods when the in-cluster `Secret` changes. `"stakater-strict"` adds the `match` annotation, and `{ secrets: [...], configMaps: [...] }` targets specific names. This is the option that works with `passthrough`, because konfig never sees the plaintext.
- `hashSecretValues({ values, salt })` from `@konfig.ts/k8s` produces a fingerprint of resolved values you can put in a pod annotation, so a re-render with new values changes the pod template and rolls the Deployment without a controller. It needs the plaintext at build time, so it pairs with `Sops.source` (or `Secret.bind({ source })`, which exposes a `values` service), not with `passthrough`.

<Aside type="caution" title="Do not commit plaintext">
The committed `SopsSecret-*.yaml` files are safe to publish only because their values are ciphertext. Keep the private age key out of the repository and out of `konfig build` unless you deliberately chose the `backend` mode.
</Aside>

The five intentionally broken files in examples/full-stack/infra/envs, what each one gets wrong, why the type checker rejects it, and how to fix it.

import { Aside, Diagnostics } from "@/components/docs"

The example project ships five files under `examples/full-stack/infra/envs/` that do not compile on purpose. Each demonstrates one class of mistake konfig.ts moves from `argocd sync` time to `tsc` time. They are part of the example's `tsconfig.json` include set and every intended error is marked with `@ts-expect-error`, so CI (`bun run --cwd examples/full-stack check`) fails if any of them ever starts compiling. The errors shown here are guaranteed to stay errors.

Two things to keep in mind when reading them:

- None of these files is listed in `konfig.json`, so `konfig build` never loads them. They exist for the type checker only.
- The `@ts-expect-error` comment sits directly above the offending line. Delete the comment and you see the raw diagnostic reproduced below each block.

## broken.ts: a module needs a provider nobody listed

`defineApi` runs `yield* Dep.Secret("ghcr-pull")` and `yield* Dep.Image("api")` inside its build, and `defineWorker` needs `Image "worker"`. The env lists only `api` and `worker` in `modules`, so `imagePulls`, `apiBuild`, and `workerBuild` are missing.

<Diagnostics case="missing-provider" />

Why it fails: `AppOfApps.fromModules` folds every module's provided and needed types; whatever is left over becomes the residual `R` channel of the returned Effect. `AppOfApps.entrypoint` accepts only an Effect whose `R` is fully satisfied and reports the leftovers through the `_konfig_unsatisfied` hint.

Fix: add the provider modules to `modules`, before the consumers. `prod.ts` is the working version of this file.

## unbound-secret.ts: an env contract with an unbound secret

`apiEnv` declares three secret members (`db`, `s3`, `jwt`). `Environment.bind` derives a required `secrets` record from the contract: one entry per secret member, and for backends whose type says `requiresSource: true`, a `source` next to the `backend`.

<Diagnostics case="unbound-secret" />

Why it fails: `BindEnvironmentInput` makes `secrets` mandatory when the environment has any secret member (`HasSecrets<M>`), types each entry as `SecretMemberOptions<N, K>` (a `backend`, a `source`, or both), and the `Sops.backend` return type is `SecretBackend<N, K, true, ...>`, whose `true` forces `source`. `Sops.passthrough` returns `SecretBackend<N, K, false, ...>`, so no `source` is required there.

Fix: bind every secret member, and pair `Sops.backend` with `Sops.source({ file, keys })`. See [Secrets with sops](/konfig.ts/docs/guides/secrets-with-sops/).

## widened-name.ts: an Application name that is not a literal

Names are the vertices of the dependency graph, so `Application.define` and every `Module.fixedNs` wrapper accept `name` and `namespace` as `Application.LiteralName<T>`. A value typed `string`, here read from `Config.string(...)`, is rejected.

<Diagnostics case="widened-name" />

Why it fails: with `name: string`, `Dep.Provide<"App", string>` would satisfy any `Dep.Need<"App", X>` and the missing-provider check above would silently pass. `LiteralName<T>` resolves to `T` for a literal and to an object carrying a `_konfig_error` message when `string extends T`, so the widened value no longer matches the parameter.

Fix: keep names literal at the call site. If a name has to vary by environment, branch on literals (`env === "prod" ? "api" : "api-staging"`) or pass the literal in from the env entry rather than reading it from process configuration inside the module.

## envname-collision.ts: two members claim one env var

`Environment.define` computes the set of `envName`s across its top-level `Secret`, `Literal`, and `Downward` members and rejects a duplicate at the type level. Nested environments are covered by the runtime check in the same call, which throws `EnvNameCollision` when the module is loaded.

<Diagnostics case="envname-collision" />

Why it fails: two members writing the same variable name would produce two `env` entries with the same `name` in the pod spec, and which value wins is a Kubernetes ordering detail. The check catches literal against literal, secret key against literal, and secret against secret.

Fix: rename one of the `envName`s (or one key in a `Secret.define` `env` map). If both members are meant to be the same value, keep one member and reference it from both places.

## app-name-collision.ts: two Applications with the same name

Two `Application.define` calls with `name: "api"` are passed to `AppOfApps.fromModules`.

<Diagnostics case="app-name-collision" />

Why it fails: `fromModules` is typed with `Compose.NoDuplicateProvides<Ms, "AppOfApps.fromModules">`. Two modules providing `App "api"` would let the later layer shadow the earlier one at runtime, and the emitted `Application-api.yaml` would be written twice with different content, so it is rejected before that can happen with a `_konfig_duplicate` hint.

Fix: give each Application a distinct name. If you want two instances of one module, call the factory twice with different `name`s (`defineApi({ name: "api" })`, `defineApi({ name: "api-canary" })`).

<Aside type="tip" title="Reproduce locally">
Run `bun run --cwd examples/full-stack check` from the repository root. It passes because every intended error is expected; remove one `@ts-expect-error` line to see the diagnostic in full.
</Aside>

External Secrets backend for konfig.ts, emitting ExternalSecret CRs that the operator reconciles from an external store.

import { Aside } from "@/components/docs"

`@konfig.ts/external-secrets` is the [External Secrets](https://external-secrets.io) backend. It emits an `ExternalSecret` CR that the External Secrets Operator reconciles into a normal `Secret` by pulling values from AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault, 1Password, and similar stores. konfig never touches the values: the backend declares `requiresSource: false`, so no plaintext source is needed at render time.

## Install

```bash
bun add @konfig.ts/external-secrets
```

## Usage

Bind a contract from `@konfig.ts/env` to the backend. `remoteRef` maps each contract key to its path in the store.

```ts title="infra/modules/db.ts"
import { ExternalSecrets } from "@konfig.ts/external-secrets"
import { Secret } from "@konfig.ts/k8s"

const dbCreds = Secret.define({
  name: "db-creds",
  namespace: "prod",
  env: { url: "DATABASE_URL", password: "DATABASE_PASSWORD" }
})

const bound = Secret.bind({
  secret: dbCreds,
  backend: ExternalSecrets.backend({
    secretStoreRef: { name: "aws-prod", kind: "ClusterSecretStore" },
    refreshInterval: "1h",
    remoteRef: (key) => ({ key: `prod/api/${key}` })
  })
})
// bound.manifest is the ExternalSecret CR
```

For a whole bundle, pass the backend to `Environment.bind({ env, namespace, secrets: { db: { backend } } })`; no `source` field is required.

| Export | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ExternalSecrets.backend` | `(opts)`: a `SecretBackend<N, K, false, ExternalSecret>` |
| `ExternalSecretsBackendOptions<K>` | `secretStoreRef` (required), `refreshInterval?` (`"1h"`, `"30m"`), `remoteRef?: (key: K) => ExternalSecretRemoteRef`, `target?` |
| `SecretStoreRef`, `SecretStoreKind` | `{ name, kind?: "SecretStore" \| "ClusterSecretStore" }` |
| `ExternalSecret`, `ExternalSecretSpec`, `ExternalSecretDataEntry`, `ExternalSecretRemoteRef`, `ExternalSecretTarget`, `ExternalSecretCreationPolicy`, `ExternalSecretDeletionPolicy` | CR types |

## Errors

This package exports no tagged error classes. It performs no I/O; failures at bind time come from the shared machinery in `@konfig.ts/k8s` and `@konfig.ts/env`.

<Aside type="note">
`secretStoreRef.kind` defaults to `SecretStore`. Use `ClusterSecretStore` for cluster-scoped stores. `remoteRef` defaults to the identity mapping, `key => { key }`.
</Aside>

Sealed Secrets backend for konfig.ts, sealing plaintext with kubeseal at render time and emitting a SealedSecret CR.

import { Aside } from "@/components/docs"

`@konfig.ts/sealed-secrets` is the [Sealed Secrets](https://github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets) backend. At render time konfig resolves a `SecretSource` to plaintext (held only as `Redacted<string>` in memory), builds a plain `Secret`, pipes it to `kubeseal` over stdin, and emits the returned `SealedSecret` CR. Only the in-cluster controller can decrypt it, so the manifest is safe to commit.

## Install

```bash
bun add @konfig.ts/sealed-secrets
```

Needs the `kubeseal` CLI on the machine that runs `konfig build`, plus the controller's public certificate: `certPath`, else the `KUBESEAL_CERT` environment variable.

## Usage

Bind a contract from `@konfig.ts/env` to the backend and give it a source for the plaintext. `requiresSource: true` makes `source` a compile-time requirement.

```ts title="infra/modules/db.ts"
import { SecretSource } from "@konfig.ts/env"
import { Secret } from "@konfig.ts/k8s"
import { SealedSecrets } from "@konfig.ts/sealed-secrets"

const dbCreds = Secret.define({
  name: "db-creds",
  namespace: "prod",
  env: { url: "DATABASE_URL", password: "DATABASE_PASSWORD" }
})

const bound = Secret.bind({
  secret: dbCreds,
  backend: SealedSecrets.backend({ scope: "strict" }),
  source: SecretSource.fromConfig({
    keys: ["url", "password"],
    envName: (k) => `DB_${k.toUpperCase()}`
  })
})
// bound.manifest is the SealedSecret CR
```

For a whole bundle, pass the same backend to `Environment.bind({ env, namespace, secrets: { db: { backend, source } } })`.

## Surface

| Export | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `SealedSecrets.backend` | `(opts?)`: a `SecretBackend<N, K, true, SealedSecret>` |
| `SealedSecretsBackendOptions` | `scope?: "strict" \| "namespace-wide" \| "cluster-wide"` (default `strict`), `certPath?` (default `$KUBESEAL_CERT`) |
| `runKubeseal`, `resolveCertPath` | Low-level helpers: run `kubeseal` on a Secret, resolve the certificate path |
| `SealedSecret`, `SealedSecretSpec`, `SealedSecretTemplate`, `SealedSecretScope` | CR types |

## Errors

- `KubesealCertMissing`: neither `certPath` nor `KUBESEAL_CERT` is set.
- `KubesealInvocationError`: `kubeseal` exited non-zero or was not found.
- `KubesealParseError`: `kubeseal` output did not decode as a `SealedSecret`.

<Aside type="caution">
`scope` must match how the controller was asked to seal: `strict` binds to name and namespace, `namespace-wide` allows renaming inside the namespace, `cluster-wide` allows any namespace.
</Aside>

SOPS secret backend for konfig.ts, emitting SopsSecret resources by passthrough or by re-encrypting resolved values to cluster recipients.

import { Aside, Snippet } from "@/components/docs"

`@konfig.ts/sops` is the [SOPS](https://github.com/getsops/sops) backend. Keep encrypted secrets in git and turn them into `SopsSecret` custom resources at render time for the in-cluster [sops-secrets-operator](https://github.com/isindir/sops-secrets-operator) to reconcile. Two modes: `Sops.passthrough` emits an already-encrypted file verbatim (offline, no decrypt), and `Sops.backend` re-encrypts resolved values to your recipients. `Sops.source` decrypts a file into a `SecretSource` you can feed to any backend.

## Install

```bash
bun add @konfig.ts/sops
```

`Sops.backend` and `Sops.source` shell out to the `sops` CLI on the machine that runs `konfig build`. Recipient credentials come from each file's own `sops:` metadata. `Sops.passthrough` needs no CLI.

## Usage

The full-stack example ships the GHCR pull secret as an encrypted `SopsSecret` file and provides it as `Dep.Secret("ghcr-pull")`.

<Snippet file="infra/modules/image-pulls.ts" startAt="export const defineImagePulls" title="infra/modules/image-pulls.ts" />

Re-encrypting mode, when the plaintext should flow through konfig:

```ts title="infra/modules/db.ts"
import { Secret } from "@konfig.ts/k8s"
import { Sops } from "@konfig.ts/sops"

const bound = Secret.bind({
  secret: dbCreds,
  backend: Sops.backend({ recipients: { age: ["age1..."] } }),
  source: Sops.source({ file: "infra/secrets/db-creds.enc.yaml", keys: ["url", "password"] })
})
```

## Surface

| Export | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `Sops.passthrough` | `({ file })`: emit the file's `SopsSecret`, restamped to the bound namespace; `requiresSource: false` |
| `Sops.backend` | `({ recipients, type? })`: re-encrypt to `age` / `kms` / `gcpKms` / `azureKv` / `pgp` recipients; `requiresSource: true` |
| `Sops.source` | `({ file, keys, extract? })`: a `SecretSource` that decrypts once and yields `Redacted` values |
| `sopsDecrypt`, `sopsEncryptStdin` | Low-level CLI wrappers |
| `SopsBackendOptions`, `SopsSourceInput`, `SopsRecipients`, `SopsSecret`, `SopsSecretSpec`, `SopsSecretTemplate` | Option and CR types |

## Errors

- `SopsInvocationError`: the `sops` process failed or was not found.
- Every emitted value is checked for the `ENC[...]` marker; a plaintext value fails the render (an internal `SopsUnencryptedValueError`) rather than emitting plaintext dressed as a secret.

<Aside type="note">
`Sops.source` composes with other backends: decrypt with SOPS, then seal with `SealedSecrets.backend` or emit a plain `NativeSecret`.
</Aside>
